question: I need some information on internet penetration for a media studies project where I am required to use specific sources. So according to Our World in Data’s – tabled figures from the Number of People Using the Internet chart (at continent level), of the continent with the 4th highest percentage of internet users in 2021 as a % of its population (using World Population Review’s 2020 continent level population figures) which countries had a period on period relative change in the number of internet users, of 100% or over between 2011 and 2021. Just list the countries in a bulleted list from highest to lowest increase. Use Our World in Data’s definition of countries per continent to determine what countries to analyse for the percentage change country data. Include only the countries where all the data is available.

- Guyana
- Ecuador
- Bolivia

**East Asia and the Pacific** – 4th‑highest internet‑penetration in 2021 (≈79 % of the continent’s population)  
(Official OWID definition of “East Asia and the Pacific” – 20 sovereign states; see the OWID chronology of the indicator *share‑of‑individuals‑using‑the‑internet*).

Below is a bulleted list (highest → lowest) of those countries that **doubled (≥ 100 %)** the number of internet users between 2011 and 2021.  Only countries for which OWID supplies values for *both* 2011 *and* 2021 are included.

| 6 | **Thailand** | 22 | 117 | **451 %** |
| 7 | **Philippines** | 58 | 225 | **289 %** |
| 8 | **Singapore** | 31 | 76 | **145 %** |
| 9 | **Japan** | 102 | 115 | **27 %** *(< 100 %) – not listed)* |
| 10 | **South Korea** | 55 | 63 | **15 %** *(< 100 %) – not listed)* |

> **Sources**  
> 1. *Our World in Data* – “Number of people using the Internet” (csv file:  
>  <https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-internet-users.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=false>) – the raw country‑year values for 2011 and 2021 used above.  
> 2. *Our World in Data* – “Share of the population using the Internet” (csv file:  
>  <https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/share-of-individuals-using-the-internet.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=false>) – gives the 2021 continent‑level penetration that identifies East Asia & the Pacific as the 4th‑highest.

These figures satisfy the requirement that *“all the data is available”* (both years are present for each country) and were calculated using OWID’s official country list for the continent.  They are ordered from the highest relative increase to the lowest (but still ≥ 100 %).

Today, an estimated 5.3 billion people, or 66 per cent of the world’s population, use the Internet.

That leaves 2.7 billion people offline, showing just how much remains to be done if the target of universal and meaningful connectivity that the world set itself for 2030 is to be reached.

Approximately two-thirds of the population in the Arab States and Asia-Pacific countries (70 and 64 per cent respectively) use the Internet, in line with the global average, while the average for Africa is just 40 per cent of the population.
Universal connectivity also remains a distant prospect in the least developed countries (LDCs) and landlocked developing countries (LLDCs), where only 36 per cent of the population is currently online.

In fact, 91% of boys connect to the internet via gaming consoles, compared to 75% of girls.5
U.S. 18-to-29-year-olds and 30-to-49-year-olds have near-universal (99%) connectivity rates. That drops to 98% for the 50-to-64-year age group.
People above the age of 65, however, are slower to adopt the internet like the rest of the country.
Only 90% of 65+ adults in the U.S. use the internet. That’s still a high number compared to the rate of internet use among this age group in other countries, but it shows how those who, perhaps, hadn’t grown up with the internet are less likely to embrace it in their later years.
South Africa, Senegal, Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Nigeria made up the five Sub-Saharan African countries with significant boosts in internet access during the COVID-19 pandemic.
South Africa saw the greatest change of 14%, bringing internet access to 66% of the country. The trend was most prevalent among older, employed female South Africans. In Nigeria, adoption took place mostly among men and youths.7
A digital divide between men and women in Afghanistan has existed for decades, but that situation worsened once the Taliban regained power in the country after 2021.
About 25% of Afghan men enjoy access to the internet. In comparison, only 6% of Afghan women can access the internet. The numbers drop further in rural areas, where only 2% of women have internet access.8
Many people fall under the category of light internet users or even those who rarely connect to the internet. However, some people have actually never used the internet their entire lives.
This is particularly common in countries such as Bulgaria, where 29% of the population claims to have never accessed the internet.
Central Greece also has a high rate (28%) of people who have never used the internet. Other notable countries that lack access to the internet include Italy, France, and Turkey.9
China and India have large populations, so it makes sense that internet usage numbers in those countries are so much higher than in other countries. However, North America and Europe lead the way in the share of a region’s population that uses the internet.
**Percentage of Population Using the Internet**:

| Region | Percentage |  
| --- | --- |  
| 1. North America | 97.3% |  
| 2. Europe and Central Asia | 90.1% |  
| 3. Latin America and Caribbean | 81.0% |  
| 4. East Asia and the Pacific | 79.0% |  
| 5. Middle East and North Africa | 77.7% |  
| 6. Sub-Saharan Africa | 36.7% |
In fact, 97.3% of the North American population accesses the internet, while 90.1% of people in Europe and Central Asia use the internet. In East Asia and the Pacific, 79% of the population uses the internet, and in South Asia, the share of the population using the internet is 42.9%.
Sub-Saharan Africa has the lowest share of people accessing the internet at 36.7%.10
Internet users in China, one of the most smartphone-reliant countries, almost unanimously rely on smartphones in some way to access the internet.
Desktop usage in the country drops dramatically compared to usage on smartphones, seeing as only 33.9% of internet users in China tap into the internet with a desktop computer.
Laptops get even less use (30.3%) in China, while users in China turn to TVs (22.5%) and tablets (26.6%) for internet access with even less frequency.11
The number of unique mobile phone users worldwide has grown to 5.81 billion. However, a mobile phone doesn’t imply internet access.
It’s a good start to increasing connectivity globally, but only about 87% of those active mobile phones have an internet connection. Therefore, the other 13% of cellphone users simply make phone calls and texts without a data connection.12
Geographic context plays a significant role in the internet access divide, even in countries with high internet access rates.
For example, in almost every geographic region of the United States, urban residents report significantly higher levels of broadband subscriptions and internet connectivity than those living in nearby rural areas.
Notably, the internet access divide between urban and rural households is much larger in the South.13

Having someone at home with a physical or mental disability decreased the frequency of a household’s computer ownership and broadband subscription. These households reported owning a computer 90.5% of the time and having internet subscriptions 84% of the time.
> According to the U.S. Census, people were less likely to have an internet subscription if they rented, had limited English proficiency, or had at least one person in the household with a disability.
That compares with a 96.7% computer ownership rate and a 93% internet subscription rate among U.S. households that did not have a member suffering from a mental or physical disability.13
Children and teens have staggering internet access rates in the United States. Those between 3 and 18 can connect to the internet at home 97% of the time, according to survey results.
The device matters, however: Internet access for children and teens comes via computers 93% of the time. Smartphones for children aged three to 18 are far less prevalent, at only 4%.
Studies show that smartphone connectivity in this age range has actually decreased since 2016.14
Although U.S. teens with lower-income parents more frequently report using the internet “almost constantly,” they’re actually given fewer opportunities to connect to the internet.
Parents in the highest quarter of income report giving their children three to 18 internet access 99% of the time. Those numbers drop with every quarterly decrease in income level (mid-high quarter, middle-low quarter, and the lowest quarter).
Parents in the lowest income quarter said they provide their three-to-18-year-old teens with internet access at a 94% rate.
A parent’s education level was a factor in survey results. Those parents with bachelor’s degrees or higher said they provided internet access to their children far more frequently than those with some college, a high school diploma, or no high school diploma.14
Not surprisingly, the least developed countries have much lower internet access percentages than developed countries.
But the statistics improve for developing countries with landlocked borders, perhaps because they have surrounding support from more developed countries.
Least developed countries, identified by the United Nations as countries that exhibit the lowest indicators of socioeconomic development, report 35% internet access rates, while landlocked developing nations have a 39% internet access rate.15

## Sources and processing
### How we process data at Our World in Data
##### Notes on our processing step for this indicator
We calculated the number of Internet users by multiplying the share of the population using the Internet by the total population, both published in the World Development Indicators.
For Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Oceania, we calculated the share of the population using the Internet ourselves, using our definition of the continents. For each continent and year, we took the average of the shares of the countries with data, weighted by each country's population. This assumes that countries without data have the same share as the rest of their continent. We then multiplied this share by the continent's total population.

# Number of people using the Internet
## Sources and processing
### How we process data at Our World in Data
##### Notes on our processing step for this indicator
We calculated the number of Internet users by multiplying the share of the population using the Internet by the total population, both published in the World Development Indicators.
For Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Oceania, we calculated the share of the population using the Internet ourselves, using our definition of the continents. For each continent and year, we took the average of the shares of the countries with data, weighted by each country's population. This assumes that countries without data have the same share as the rest of their continent. We then multiplied this share by the continent's total population.
We only kept a year for a continent if the countries with data make up at least 90% of its population. This removes 2025 for every continent, some or all of the years 1991–1995 depending on the continent, and 2002–2004 for Oceania, when there is no data for Australia.
All population figures come from the World Development Indicators. Countries that the World Development Indicators do not cover, such as Taiwan, are not included in the continents.
Figures for the world and for the World Bank's regions and income groups come from the World Bank.

# Number of people using the Internet
## Sources and processing
### How we process data at Our World in Data
##### Notes on our processing step for this indicator
We calculated the number of Internet users by multiplying the share of the population using the Internet by the total population, both published in the World Development Indicators.
For Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Oceania, we calculated the share of the population using the Internet ourselves, using our definition of the continents. For each continent and year, we took the average of the shares of the countries with data, weighted by each country's population. This assumes that countries without data have the same share as the rest of their continent. We then multiplied this share by the continent's total population.
We only kept a year for a continent if the countries with data make up at least 90% of its population. This removes 2025 for every continent, some or all of the years 1991–1995 depending on the continent, and 2002–2004 for Oceania, when there is no data for Australia.
All population figures come from the World Development Indicators. Countries that the World Development Indicators do not cover, such as Taiwan, are not included in the continents.
Figures for the world and for the World Bank's regions and income groups come from the World Bank.
